chapters.title: Chapter 1: Federal Circuit Appellate Jurisdiction and Choice of Law
chapters.description: Explains when and how the Federal Circuit reviews patent cases from district courts and which body of law governs different issues on appeal.
subtopics: 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1) and the scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction
Final judgment rule and appealability
Applying regional circuit law to procedural issues (e.g., JMOL, new trial)
Applying Federal Circuit law to patent-specific issues
Standards for granting costs on appeal

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Standards of Review in Patent Appeals
chapters.description: Details the distinct standards of review that structure appellate analysis in patent cases.
subtopics: De novo review of JMOL decisions under regional circuit law
Substantial evidence review for jury findings of infringement and damages
De novo review of claim construction with clear-error review for subsidiary fact findings (Teva framework)
Abuse of discretion review for new-trial rulings
Harmless error principles

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Rule 50 JMOL and Rule 59 New Trial
chapters.description: Covers the mechanics and strategic considerations for post-trial motions challenging jury verdicts.
subtopics: Rule 50(a) pre-verdict motions and issue preservation
Rule 50(b) renewed JMOL requirements and scope
Rule 59 motions for new trial: grounds and standards
Waiver and forfeiture tied to Rule 50 timing
Appellate remedies after JMOL and new-trial rulings

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Patent Infringement Basics—Elements, Burdens, and Theories
chapters.description: Introduces the substantive law of patent infringement with emphasis on proving literal infringement of method claims.
subtopics: 35 U.S.C. § 271 and types of infringement
All-elements rule and element-by-element proof
Literal infringement vs. doctrine of equivalents (overview)
Direct infringement of method claims and performance of each step
Burden of proof (preponderance) and presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. § 282)

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Claim Construction Fundamentals
chapters.description: Explains how courts determine the meaning of claim terms prior to infringement analysis.
subtopics: Phillips hierarchy: claim language, specification, prosecution history
Role and limits of extrinsic evidence (e.g., inventor testimony, textbooks)
Markman hearings and timing relative to trial
Teva: factual underpinnings of claim construction and appellate review
Construing structural vs. functional language; ‘wherein’ clauses

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Prosecution History, Disclaimer, and Estoppel
chapters.description: Addresses how statements and amendments during prosecution can affect claim scope.
subtopics: Prosecution disclaimer/disavowal in claim construction
Requirement of clear and unambiguous statements to limit scope
Distinguishing disclaimer from prosecution history estoppel (DOE context)
Weight of examiner statements vs. applicant statements
Reliance on intrinsic vs. extrinsic evidence in assessing disclaimer

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Expert Testimony in Patent Cases
chapters.description: Outlines the admissibility and use of expert testimony to prove infringement and damages.
subtopics: Federal Rules of Evidence 702 and Daubert reliability
Rule 703: reliance on technical materials and company documents
Mapping claim limitations to accused products
Use of demonstratives and tutorials
Handling inconsistencies and the effect of self-contradictory testimony

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Evidence Sufficiency and the Substantial-Evidence Standard
chapters.description: Clarifies what constitutes legally sufficient evidence to sustain a jury verdict in patent cases.
subtopics: Defining substantial evidence and the reasonable-jury test
Documentary vs. testimonial proof in complex technology cases
Bridging the inferential gap: need for clear mappings and explanations
Impact of contradictions, speculation, and conclusory assertions
Interplay between sufficiency review and JMOL

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Patent Remedies—Reasonable Royalty and Damages Proof
chapters.description: Presents the framework for calculating patent damages and common evidentiary pitfalls.
subtopics: 35 U.S.C. § 284 and the reasonable royalty floor
Georgia-Pacific factors and the hypothetical negotiation
Lump-sum vs. running royalties; convoyed sales and apportionment
Entire market value rule and smallest saleable unit
Standards for new trial on damages and vacatur when liability is reversed

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Method Claims in Communication and Signal-Processing Technologies
chapters.description: Provides context for analyzing method claims involving digital signal processing in radio/telecom systems.
subtopics: Common claim structures for sampling, filtering, and digital multiplication
Hardware/firmware/software implementations (e.g., FPGAs, DSPs)
Interpreting mathematical operations (e.g., modulus, conjugates) in claims
Direct performance vs. capability; single-actor performance of steps
Proving operation using technical schematics and algorithm descriptions

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Using Technical Documentation to Prove Infringement
chapters.description: Explains best practices for relying on internal product documents and diagrams to meet claim elements.
subtopics: Authenticating and interpreting engineering diagrams and block charts
Correlating nomenclature in documents to claim terms
Mathematical notation and signal labels as evidentiary proof
Avoiding misreads and clarifying ambiguous legends or labels
Linking documents to actual operation, not just design goals

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Appellate Remedies—Reversal, Vacatur, and Remand
chapters.description: Describes the forms of appellate relief available and their practical consequences for liability and damages.
subtopics: Reversal vs. vacatur vs. remand
Effect of reversing liability on damages awards
Scope of remand instructions
Entry of judgment as a matter of law vs. ordering a new trial
Allocation of costs on appeal

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Landmark Doctrines—Wi-LAN, Inc. v. Apple Inc.
chapters.description: Reviews how this decision frames standards of review in patent jury cases, including application of regional circuit law to JMOL and mixed standards for claim construction.
subtopics: De novo review of JMOL under regional circuit precedent
Substantial evidence for jury verdicts in patent cases
Claim construction review after Teva
Practical impact on structuring appellate arguments

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Landmark Doctrines—Apple Inc. v. Wi-LAN Inc.
chapters.description: Focuses on the substantial-evidence standard for sustaining or overturning jury findings on infringement and damages.
subtopics: Defining substantial evidence in the patent context
Evaluating expert mappings and documentary support
Limits of conclusory testimony
Guidance on preserving sufficiency challenges

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Landmark Doctrines—Johns Hopkins University v. Datascope Corp.
chapters.description: Explains how self-contradictory expert testimony affects the sufficiency of evidence to support a verdict.
subtopics: When contradictions render testimony insufficient as a matter of law
Reconciling conflicting expert statements
Interaction with the all-elements rule
Strategic cross-examination and record-building

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Landmark Doctrines—Continental Circuits LLC v. Intel Corp.
chapters.description: Covers the high bar for finding prosecution disclaimer or disavowal and the primacy of intrinsic evidence.
subtopics: Clear and unambiguous requirement for disclaimer
Caution in using inventor testimony to narrow claims
Distinguishing mere amendment from limiting disavowal
Using prosecution history without overreading examiner citations
